A1.notes.Q3: I'm cautious about privacy, especially with sensitive data. Moderate gains are acceptable if the benefit to students is clear. Fairness is key - we shouldn’t exacerbate inequalities.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust with students and ensuring we provide appropriate support. A black box model isn't helpful; advisors need to understand the reasoning.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital, but a small reduction in overall identification is acceptable if it means equity across groups. It's ethically important to avoid perpetuating existing disadvantages.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is best, but we need to respect student time and avoid overwhelming them. A meeting allows for more in-depth conversation. Twice a year feels manageable.
A1.notes.Q7: I’d prefer slightly fewer contacts, if personalization is involved. Fewer but higher quality interactions are more useful than spamming students with generic messages.
A1.Q8.1: It would be helpful to understand how the model will account for extenuating circumstances – illness, personal crises etc. We need a process to override flags when appropriate.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, especially with sensitive data. First-gen/Financial aid could be useful for targeted support *if* fairness can be ensured.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for building trust with students. A black box isn't helpful; we need to understand *why* a student is flagged.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. Sacrificing some overall accuracy to avoid exacerbating existing inequalities seems ethically necessary.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is key, but it needs to be done sensitively. An invitation for a meeting allows students agency.
A2.notes.Q7: Personalized interventions require more care; avoid overwhelming advisors with false positives. Prioritize quality over quantity.
A2.Q8.1: A critical consideration is the training data itself. Are there biases inherent in past student outcomes that the model might perpetuate?

A3.notes.Q3: Balancing privacy is crucial, especially with sensitive data. First-gen/Financial aid could be helpful, but only if it doesn’t worsen existing inequities.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for building trust with students and being able to appropriately advise them, even if it means slightly lower accuracy.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness must be a priority. Accepting some loss of overall identification is necessary for equitable support across all student groups; recall is key to reach those who need help.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach followed by an option to discuss things further seems best. Too much contact could be intrusive. Twice a year is reasonable.
A3.notes.Q7: With general info, many contacts are okay – it’s low stakes. Personalized emails need to be carefully targeted; we don't want to waste student or advisor time.
A3.Q8.1: The model should be regularly audited for bias and effectiveness, ensuring it continues to support all students fairly. Advisor workload needs consideration if the model increases contacts.

S1.notes.Q3: Privacy is really important, especially with sensitive data. First-generation and financial aid status seem less *inherently* private, but still need justification for inclusion.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial, especially after my own dropout experience. I'd want to understand *why* a system flagged me. Losing accuracy for transparency feels worth it up to a point.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness is key, but missing students who need help isn't acceptable. A small decrease in overall identification for better equality seems reasonable – we shouldn’t perpetuate existing disadvantages.
S1.notes.Q6: A generic email feels impersonal, and a meeting is helpful *if* the student wants it. Twice a year seems frequent enough without being overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: More targeted intervention warrants fewer false positives. A personalized email has more value, so slightly fewer students contacted overall is acceptable.
S1.Q8.1: It feels important to have clear opt-out options for the entire system, and transparency about how data is used and secured. Students should be able to easily access their data.

S2.notes.Q3: Privacy is vital, especially for sensitive data. Only use if it significantly helps and doesn’t disproportionately affect certain groups.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for building trust and supporting students effectively. Some loss of accuracy is acceptable for clarity.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial, even if it means identifying slightly fewer students overall. Missing vulnerable groups is unacceptable.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but requires resources. Twice-yearly check-ins seem reasonable and not overly intrusive.
S2.notes.Q7: More targeted outreach with personalized emails warrants a slightly more conservative approach to avoid overwhelming students.
S2.Q8.1: The model should include provisions for false positives – a process where incorrectly flagged students can easily clarify their situation and are not penalized. Also, ensure transparency about the data used and how the model works.

S3.notes.Q3: Data privacy is crucial, especially regarding sensitive attributes. Disability info is acceptable if it improves fairness, but needs strong safeguards.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust & appropriate support. A slightly less accurate but explainable model is preferable to a ‘black box’.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital, but shouldn't come at the expense of helping *anyone*. A small reduction in overall accuracy for fairer outcomes is acceptable.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized support & an invitation to discuss issues are ideal. Too much contact could be intrusive; twice a year feels reasonable.
S3.notes.Q7: Generic emails can reach more students, personalized ones require careful handling. Fewer proactive touches for personalised outreach is preferable.
S3.Q8.1: The model needs to be regularly audited to ensure it isn't perpetuating existing biases and consider the intersectionality of student experiences.

S4.notes.Q3: Privacy is really important, but disability data *could* be useful if handled incredibly carefully and anonymized properly. Otherwise too risky.
S4.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, especially for students who might already feel vulnerable. Losing too much accuracy for it isn't worth it though.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness has to be a priority, even if the overall numbers go down. The system shouldn’t exacerbate existing inequalities. Prioritizing recall is crucial.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails are useless. Personalized outreach, ideally with an invitation to talk things through is best. Not constantly though - could feel overwhelming.
S4.notes.Q7: Personalized contact requires more careful consideration – avoid unnecessary stress. More selective here makes sense than with the general email approach.
S4.Q8.1: The biggest concern is that this system *feels* punitive, not supportive. It needs to be very clearly framed as help and not surveillance.

S5.notes.Q3: I’m wary of using too much personal data, but understanding background might help. Nationality could be relevant given I’m an international student.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially as a new student navigating a different system. I'd want to understand *why* any flag occurred.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. A slightly less accurate model that doesn’t perpetuate inequalities is better. It's important to find those who need help.
S5.notes.Q6: I’d prefer initial contact to be less intrusive (email), with an option for more personalized help if I wanted it. Twice a year seems reasonable.
S5.notes.Q7: With general information, contacting more is okay. But with personalized info, be careful about bothering students who are doing fine.
S5.Q8.1: It would be helpful to know what the criteria for 'academic difficulty' actually *are*. Is it just grades or other factors like engagement?

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is really important, but some data *could* help without being too invasive. Nationality and first-gen status are okay if it improves fairness.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, especially at the higher levels. If I don’t understand *why* a system flags me, it feels unfair and unhelpful. Less explainability just isn't worth it.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital. Missing students from marginalized groups would be worse than a slight dip in overall accuracy. It’s about equity, not just efficiency.
S6.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal. A personalized approach or invitation to meet shows actual care. Twice a year feels right; continuous contact is too much.
S6.notes.Q7: With just general info, it’s okay to reach out more broadly. But with personalized contact, it needs to be targeted to avoid wasting resources and causing anxiety.
S6.Q8.1: It would be good to know how the model is audited for bias regularly, and what steps are taken if biases are detected.

S7.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, especially with sensitive data. Disability info *could* be useful for targeted support but needs careful handling.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial, but I'm willing to trade some for significantly better identification. Less explanation if it helps more people.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness *has* to be a priority, even at the cost of slightly fewer overall identifications. Missing students from marginalised groups is worse.
S7.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but needs to be delivered sensitively. Too much contact can be counterproductive.
S7.notes.Q7: With a general email, reaching out more widely makes sense. But with personalized emails it's important not to waste advisor time or bother students unnecessarily.
S7.Q8.1: It’s crucial that any identified support is *actually* helpful and accessible to all students, including those with disabilities like mine. Simply flagging isn’t enough.

S8.notes.Q3: Data privacy is paramount, especially sensitive info. First-generation status/finance could be relevant but with careful consideration for bias.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust and effective support. Lower explainability erodes that, even with improved accuracy.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness matters hugely. A small dip in overall accuracy is acceptable to ensure equitable support for all students, especially marginalized ones.
S8.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is better than generic, but needs to be respectful and invite voluntary engagement. Twice a year feels balanced.
S8.notes.Q7: With general emails, fewer false positives are okay. Personalized messages require more precision - balance is key to avoid overwhelming advisors.
S8.Q8.1: The system should be opt-out rather than opt-in. Students should have agency over their data and involvement. Also, ensure culturally sensitive support services are available.

S9.notes.Q3: I'm very wary of data collection, especially personal details. Small improvements are okay if it genuinely helps, but privacy is paramount. Disability and nationality require extra care.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust, especially given my own experiences navigating university support. Less explainable models feel like a black box and are unacceptable.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness should be prioritized even if it means slightly lower overall accuracy. Missing vulnerable students is unacceptable, especially if the model perpetuates inequalities.
S9.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but should be optional and not overly intrusive. Twice a year feels like a good balance between checking in and giving space.
S9.notes.Q7: Generic emails can feel dismissive. Personalised follow-ups are more important, even if it means contacting fewer people overall. A balance is needed.
S9.Q8.1: The model needs clear opt-out options for students. Also, any outreach must be sensitive to the fact that mental health conditions or past failures can make seeking help difficult.
